title: How do airlines make money, and what matters in an airline case?
description: Airline economics for case interviews: load factor, yield, cost per seat-mile, fixed costs and ancillary revenue, with a worked break-even load factor.
hook: Airlines appear in case interviews constantly because their economics are so clear: expensive planes, mostly fixed costs, and profit that swings with how full each flight is. Learn a handful of measures and airline cases become much easier.
body:
How airlines make money

Ticket revenue, plus a growing share from ancillaries: bags, seat choice, food and loyalty programmes, where banks pay airlines for points on co-branded credit cards.

The measures that matter

  • Load factor: the share of seats filled.
  • Yield: average revenue per passenger per mile.
  • Cost per available seat-mile: the cost of flying one seat one mile, full or empty.

Why fixed costs dominate

Planes, crews, airport slots and maintenance cost roughly the same whether a flight is full or not. So the last few passengers on a flight are almost pure profit, and a small drop in load factor can wipe out profit (see operating leverage).

A worked example: break-even load factor

A 180-seat flight costs £18,000 to operate. The average fare is £125. Break-even passengers: £18,000 ÷ £125 = 144. Break-even load factor: 144 ÷ 180 = 80%. If the airline usually fills 85%, a fall to 78% turns every flight into a loss.

Typical airline case questions

  • Should we launch a new route? (demand, yield, cost per flight, competition, slots)
  • Why are profits falling? (fuel, load factor, price war)
  • How can we grow ancillary revenue?
  • Why are our planes slower to turn around than rivals'? (an operations case)

Work through the economics of one route

An airline is considering a new daily flight with 180 seats. Assume an average one-way fare of £125, 80% average load factor and £15 of ancillary revenue per passenger. Revenue per departure is 180 × 80% × (£125 + £15) = £20,160. If fuel, crew, landing charges, maintenance and the allocated cost of aircraft ownership total £18,000 for that departure, the flight generates about £2,160 before costs not included in that estimate.

The important comparison is revenue per available seat versus cost per available seat, not revenue per passenger alone. In the example, revenue per available seat is £112; cost per available seat is £100. If the load factor drops to 70%, revenue falls to £17,640 while most departure costs remain, turning the route unprofitable on these assumptions. You can calculate the approximate break-even load factor: £18,000 ÷ [180 × £140] = 71.4%.

Before recommending launch, ask whether the airline has suitable slots and aircraft, whether demand is seasonal, whether passengers are connecting from other flights and whether the new route takes customers from existing ones. A low headline fare might still work with strong ancillary spending; a high fare may fail if the aircraft flies half empty. The best next data request is a forecast of passengers and fare yield by month, not a national average passenger number.

A question to practise

A carrier's revenue per passenger has increased, but route profit has fallen. What three explanations would you investigate? Consider changes in fuel cost, aircraft utilisation and passenger mix before deciding that the airline needs more ticket revenue.
